description: Recognition track: reshape pipelines. Pivot with duplicate keys, three wide-to-long idioms compared. Companion to the Foundations Reshaping chapter.

tasks.title: Pivot With Duplicate Keys

description.context: Pandas has two reshape methods that look similar but behave differently when keys repeat. pivot() requires the (index, columns) pair to be UNIQUE — if any two rows share the same combination it has no rule to pick a single cell value, so it raises ValueError. pivot_table() is the aggregating cousin: it accepts duplicate keys and applies an aggfunc (default 'mean') to combine them. So pivot is for already-unique long data, pivot_table is for data that needs aggregation as part of the reshape. The error pivot raises is the engine refusing to silently choose between conflicting values.
description.task: What happens when this pivot() call runs against the 5-row dataset?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 5-row sample with a duplicate (meter_id, date) pair: M-002 has two readings on 2026-03-01.

fields.label: What happens when this pivot() call runs against the 5-row dataset?
options: Returns a wide DataFrame; M-002's 2026-03-01 cell holds 3210.0 — pivot() resolves duplicates by last-write-wins (SQL UPDATE-style), silently overwriting the first reading.
Returns a wide DataFrame; M-002's 2026-03-01 cell holds 6410.0 — pivot() sums duplicate (index, columns) pairs by default to preserve total energy across re-reads.

Raises ValueError ('Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape') — pivot() requires (index, columns) to be unique and refuses to silently choose between the two M-002/2026-03-01 values. Use pivot_table() if aggregation is intended.
Returns a wide DataFrame; M-002's 2026-03-01 cell holds the Python list [3200.0, 3210.0] — pivot() collects duplicates into an array so no value is lost.
fields.correctAnswer: Raises ValueError ('Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape') — pivot() requires (index, columns) to be unique and refuses to silently choose between the two M-002/2026-03-01 values. Use pivot_table() if aggregation is intended.
fields.rationale: pivot() raises ValueError when the (index, columns) pair is not unique. It refuses to silently pick a winner because there is no single correct answer in the data. The fix is either to deduplicate beforehand or to call pivot_table(..., aggfunc=...) which combines duplicates explicitly. The most common Junior confusion is assuming pivot picks last-write-wins (a SQL UPDATE-style mental model) or silently sums (confusing pivot with pivot_table) — Pandas chose the safest behavior, which is to fail loud.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Imports a SQL UPDATE last-write-wins rule. Pandas pivot has no such rule — it refuses to choose.

Option B: Confuses pivot with pivot_table; pivot_table's default aggfunc is 'mean' not 'sum' anyway, so the value would be 3205.0.

Option D: Invents a list-collection behavior. No mainstream pivot operation changes the cell type to a list.

tasks.title: Three Ways To Go Wide-To-Long

description.context: Wide-to-long reshape (also called 'unpivot' or 'melt') turns N value-columns into a single value-column with N times more rows. Different tools have different defaults for what to do with NULL cells in the source. Pandas melt() KEEPS them: every (id, value_var) pair produces an output row even if the value is null. Pandas stack() DROPS them by default — its dropna parameter defaults to True, so null cells are silently removed. SQL UNPIVOT is engine-dependent: DuckDB keeps nulls; some other dialects (older T-SQL) drop them by default and require INCLUDE NULLS to retain them. So 'unpivot' is not a single behavior — three idioms can produce three different row counts.
description.task: How do the three idioms differ in their handling of the null cells (M-002.Tue and M-003.Mon)?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 3-row wide-format sample. M-001 has all three days, M-002 has Tuesday null, M-003 has Monday null.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Three idioms targeting the same wide-to-long reshape.

# Idiom A — Pandas melt()
result_a = df.melt(id_vars=['meter_id'], value_vars=['Mon','Tue','Wed'],
                   var_name='date', value_name='daily_kw')

# Idiom B — Pandas stack() with reset_index
result_b = df.set_index('meter_id')[['Mon','Tue','Wed']].stack().reset_index()
result_b.columns = ['meter_id', 'date', 'daily_kw']

# Idiom C — SQL UNPIVOT (DuckDB syntax, run on the same data via a SQL engine)
# UNPIVOT df ON Mon, Tue, Wed INTO NAME date VALUE daily_kw

fields.label: How do the three idioms differ in their handling of the null cells (M-002.Tue and M-003.Mon)?
options: All three keep the null rows — reshape operations universally preserve every input cell, so all three idioms produce 9 rows (3 meters x 3 days) with two of those rows holding null daily_kw values.
All three drop the null rows — reshape operations universally treat nulls as 'no observation' and exclude them, so all three idioms produce 7 rows on this dataset.

Idiom A (melt) keeps nulls (9 rows), idiom B (stack) drops them silently because stack's dropna parameter defaults to True (7 rows), and idiom C is engine-dependent — DuckDB UNPIVOT keeps nulls; some SQL dialects drop them by default.
Idiom B (stack) keeps nulls, idiom A (melt) drops them silently, and idiom C raises an error — Pandas melt filters nulls and SQL UNPIVOT requires a non-null source by spec.
fields.correctAnswer: Idiom A (melt) keeps nulls (9 rows), idiom B (stack) drops them silently because stack's dropna parameter defaults to True (7 rows), and idiom C is engine-dependent — DuckDB UNPIVOT keeps nulls; some SQL dialects drop them by default.
fields.rationale: melt() preserves null cells — every (id, value_var) combination produces an output row regardless of value. Idiom A gives 9 rows (3 meters x 3 days) with two nulls. stack() defaults to dropna=True, so it silently drops the two null cells; idiom B gives 7 rows. SQL UNPIVOT differs by engine: DuckDB and modern T-SQL keep nulls; older dialects drop them and require INCLUDE NULLS. The most common Junior confusion is assuming 'unpivot' is a single behavior across tools — null-handling defaults are NOT interchangeable.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Believes all reshape ops preserve all input cells. stack() drops nulls by default — the universal-preservation rule is wrong.

Option B: Believes all reshape ops drop nulls. melt() does not drop them — applying a half-rule everywhere.

Option D: Reverses melt vs stack. Remembers 'one of them drops nulls' but assigns it to the wrong method.
